title: FOMO and chasing
teaches: FOMO, the fear of missing a move, makes you chase (buy late, far past your planned entry, with more risk per share) or jump in before your signal; the cure is an entry and stop written before the open and, if you miss it, a pullback that holds a higher low or the next setup.

walkthroughs.title: What FOMO is
steps: FOMO, the fear of missing out. A stock's ripping, you're on the sidelines, and it feels like you have to be in.
Everybody feels it. The urgency is what hurts you, because it pushes you into fast calls with no plan.
It shows up two ways. You buy late, way after the move. Or you jump in before your trigger.

walkthroughs.title: What a chase costs
steps: Your stop sits where the idea is wrong. Buy higher and you're just further from it.
Risk per share is entry minus stop. Every dollar you chase gets added right onto it.
Keep your size and you risk more than you planned. We keep the risk, so a chase just buys you fewer shares.
Our line is 4%. More than 4% above the buy point, we don't touch it.

walkthroughs.title: The cure
steps: Write the entry, stop and size before the open, while you're calm. Then at the open you just execute.
If you missed it, wait for a pullback that holds a higher low. Then buy that with a tight stop.
Or let it go. I'd rather miss it than chase it. Another setup always comes along.

questions.q: Your buddy texts you "major FOMO on this one" while a stock rips. What's he actually afraid of?
choices: Being left out of the move
Losing money on the trade
Buying right at the high
Holding it over the weekend
questions.answer: Being left out of the move
questions.why: Being left out. FOMO is the fear of missing out, and in trading it's the fear of missing a move. Something exciting is happening, you're on the sidelines, and you feel like you have to be in it right now. Notice it's not fear of losing. It's fear of a gain you don't have. That's what makes it dangerous. It pushes you to buy fast, with no plan, often after the move.
questions.lesson_line: FOMO wants you in right now, on somebody else's move.

wrong.Losing money on the trade: That's fear of loss. FOMO is about a gain you're not in.
wrong.Buying right at the high: Close to the opposite. FOMO is what gets you buying the high.
wrong.Holding it over the weekend: That's gap worry on a stock you own. FOMO is about one you don't.

questions.simple: FOMO is the fear of being left out of a move, and that itch pushes you into rushed buys.

reasons: +1 fixed before (checker changed the why and a distractor)

questions.q: It ran well past your planned entry, and you bought it anyway, way up there. That's a chase.
questions.why: True, that's a chase. You came in late, after the move already happened, and paid up for it. Here's what it costs you. Your stop's still down where the idea is wrong, so you're further from it. More risk on every share. And you're often buying from the people who got in early, sometimes right as it's ready to turn. Come in that late and there's not much left for you.
questions.lesson_line: If the move already ran without you, paying up for it is a chase.
questions.simple: True. Buying after the move already ran is a chase, and it leaves you far from your stop.

reasons: +1 fixed before (lesson line and facts changed by the checker)

deeper.example: Schwab describes chasing as jumping on a move after it has already happened, perhaps right when it is ready to reverse. Investopedia ties chasing to herd instinct and buying at a high price. Brett Steenbarger coached a trader who chased moves that ran from his ideal entry, and all too often it led to paper-cut losses.

questions.q: FOMO can also get you in too early, before your setup has even triggered.
questions.why: True. FOMO cuts both ways. Late is the chase. Early is buying before the trigger because you're scared it'll leave without you. Problem is, a setup that hasn't triggered hasn't proven anything yet. Set an alert at your trigger and wait for price to trade through it. If it never gets there, you never needed to own it.
questions.lesson_line: Getting in before your own signal is FOMO too. Let the trigger pull you in.
questions.simple: True. Buying before your trigger is FOMO too, just early instead of late.

reasons: +1 fixed before (lesson line changed by the checker)

deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger describes a trader who front-ran his setups, getting into trades before proper signals. Investopedia's breakout advice says the same: a good candidate is no reason to take the trade early, so wait for the price to make its move.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits.
questions.sentence: In an uptrend, each pullback stops above the last pullback's bottom. That's a higher ___.
questions.why: Low. An uptrend is a series of rising peaks and rising troughs: higher highs and higher lows. A pullback that stops above the last pullback's bottom makes a higher low. A higher high is the other half of the pattern: a new peak above the last peak, not a pullback's bottom.
questions.lesson_line: Higher highs and higher lows. That's what an uptrend is made of.
questions.simple: Low, because in an uptrend each dip stops above the last dip, and that makes a higher low.

reasons: +1 fixed before (sentence changed by the checker to remove a giveaway)

questions.q: Late to the trigger, you fill well above your planned entry and leave the stop where it was. What just changed?
choices: Your risk per share got bigger
Nothing, the stop still caps it
More room, so it's safer now
More upside to your target
questions.answer: Your risk per share got bigger
questions.why: Your risk per share got bigger. Risk per share is your entry minus your stop. The stop didn't move, your entry did, so the gap between them grew. Keep your normal share count and you're now risking more dollars than you planned. That's how a chase quietly blows up your risk. The fix: keep the dollar risk the same and buy fewer shares. And past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy it at all.
questions.lesson_line: Every dollar you chase gets added to your risk per share.

wrong.Nothing, the stop still caps it: The stop sets your exit price, not your loss per share. Buy higher and the drop to it gets longer.
wrong.More room, so it's safer now: More room is more you lose per share. The stop's where it always was, you just paid more.
wrong.More upside to your target: The other way round. A higher entry leaves less room up to the same target.

questions.simple: Your risk per share got bigger, because the gap between what you paid and your stop is wider now.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28: chasing costs size, not risk)

questions.q: A stock trades through your trigger on a strong day, and you buy it right there. That's chasing.
questions.why: False. That's the plan working. Buying strength right at your trigger is exactly what we're after. A chase is something else: buying late, way past the buy point, because you're scared to miss more. Our line is 4%. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Inside it, you're buying strength. Past it, the stop's too far away and the shares get small.
questions.lesson_line: Buying strength at your trigger is a plan. Buying it far past the trigger is a chase.
questions.simple: False. Buying at your trigger is the plan, and chasing is buying late, far past it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% line)

deeper.example: Richard Rhodes' trading rules on ChartSchool say buy what is showing strength. IBD makes the other half of the point: the further past the buy point you get in, the greater the risk of getting shaken out.

questions.q: Sunday night you write down the entry, stop and size for every name on your list. What's that really for?
choices: Deciding while you're still calm
So you never take a losing trade
So a fast move can't leave you
So you know where it goes next
questions.why: Deciding while you're calm. Once the bell rings and something's ripping, nobody thinks straight. The plan you wrote the night before is the calm version of you making the call. Then you just follow it. It won't stop losses, and you'll still miss moves. What it stops is the spur-of-the-moment buy near a high. That's why every buy we make has its entry, stop and size written down before the open.
questions.lesson_line: Make the call while you're calm. Then just follow it.

wrong.So you never take a losing trade: A plan still has losers. Stick to it and you take them small and quick.
wrong.So a fast move can't leave you: You'll still miss moves. The plan just keeps you from chasing one on the spur of the moment.
wrong.So you know where it goes next: A plan decides what you'll do. It can't tell you where the stock goes.

questions.simple: Writing it down first means you decide while calm, not in the middle of a fast move.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, written before the open)

questions.q: Plan: buy $30, stop $29. FOMO kicks in and you chase it to $33, same stop. Your risk per share is how many times the plan's?
questions.why: 4 times. The plan risked $30 minus $29, so $1 a share. The chase risks $33 minus $29, so $4 a share. 4 over 1 is 4. Same stop, four times the risk on every share. Keep your size and a normal loss turns into a big one. Keep your dollar risk and you get a quarter of the shares. Either way the chase costs you. And $33 is well past 4% above $30, so I'd let this one go.
questions.lesson_line: Chasing doesn't move your stop. It just stretches your risk per share.
questions.simple: 4 times. Your stop sat $1 under the plan price, but $4 under where you actually bought.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28: chasing costs size, not risk)
+1 fixed before (question wording changed by the checker)

choices: 3 times
0.25 times
1.1 times
4 times

wrong.3 times: That's 33 less 30, the two prices. Compare the two risks instead.
wrong.1.1 times: That's one price over the other, not the two risks.
wrong.0.25 times: Flipped it. The chase is the bigger risk, not the smaller one.

questions.q: Half your group chat just bought the same stock. That alone is reason enough for you to buy it too.
questions.why: False. Their buying gives you no entry and no stop. It's a feeling, not a setup. Following a crowd into a stock is how a lot of people end up holding the top. If it's a real setup, it'll be on your list with a trigger and a stop. If it isn't, let them have it. Nobody's making you buy just because they did.
questions.lesson_line: The crowd buying is a feeling, not a setup.
questions.simple: False. Other people buying is pressure, not a setup, and following the crowd can lead to big losses.

reasons: +1 fixed before (a fact removed by the checker)

deeper.example: The SEC's investor alerts say it plainly: others buying doesn't mean you have to, and following the crowd may lead to significant investment losses.

questions.story: Your plan is to buy a break over $25.40. It's at $25.10 and climbing fast, and you're scared it leaves without you.
questions.q: Where do you get in?
choices: Only once it clears $25.40
Right now, before it runs
Right now, $25.10 is close
Half now, half at $25.40
questions.why: Only once it clears $25.40. Buying at $25.10 is FOMO, just early. The level's there for a reason: the break over it is what you're buying. Until it trades through, there's no setup yet. If it never clears, you never owned a stock that failed to trigger. If it does, you're in at your price with the stop you planned. Market order as it goes through, full size, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Let the trigger pull you in. If it never triggers, you never needed it.

wrong.Right now, before it runs: That's getting in ahead of the setup, on fear. If the break fails, you own a stock that never triggered.
wrong.Right now, $25.10 is close: Close isn't the signal. The break over $25.40 is the whole setup.
wrong.Half now, half at $25.40: Half early is still in before the signal. We put the full size on at one price, with one stop.

questions.simple: Wait for $25.40. Buying before the trigger is fear talking, not the plan.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5 for the half-now choice)
+1 key reworded in this batch (no order type, no lone wait choice)

questions.story: You planned 200 shares at $40, stop $38. That's $400 at risk. It opens at $43 and you buy the 200 shares anyway.
questions.q: Same stop. How much are you really risking now?
questions.why: $1,000. $43 minus $38 is $5 a share. 200 shares times $5 is $1,000. That's two and a half times the $400 you signed up for, and nothing about the setup got better. You just paid more. Since the size comes from the stop, the right move was fewer shares. Better yet, pass. At $43 you're well past 4% above the $40 buy point, and we don't buy up there.
questions.lesson_line: Keep the size on a chase and the risk grows. Past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy.

wrong.$400: That was the plan at $40. Buying higher with the same stop raised the risk on every share.
wrong.$600: That's only the extra you paid over $40. The stop's still at $38, under your old entry too.
wrong.$8,600: That's the whole position. You'd only lose all of it if the stock went to zero.

questions.simple: $1,000, because every one of the 200 shares now sits $5 above the $38 stop.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 and A5: size from the stop)

questions.q: A chat room post says "get in NOW, this won't last." That kind of urgency is a good reason to move fast.
questions.why: False. Urgency is the sales pitch. "It won't last" is the oldest pressure line there is. Pump-and-dump crews use it to whip up a buying frenzy, then sell their shares into it. Nothing good in this business needs you in within the minute. We never take a trade off an alert or a post without our own entry, stop and size. So slow down and run it through your plan, or pass.
questions.lesson_line: Urgency is someone else's plan for your money. Slow down.
questions.simple: False. A rush to get in now is a pressure tactic, so slow down and use your own plan.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F66, no trades from alerts or posts)

deeper.example: The SEC warns that people pushing a stock may tell you the opportunity won't last long, to pressure you into investing right away. Its advice: never feel pressured to invest right away.

questions.q: On our Kicker setup, what's the day-one entry besides a break of the prior day's high?
choices: The 30-minute opening range break
The first trade at the opening bell
The close of the first day
Any dip below the open price
questions.why: The 30-minute opening range break. Our Kicker entry is over the previous day's high, or the day-one break of the 30-minute opening range. A level triggers the buy, not the urge.
questions.lesson_line: Even on a hot gap, a level does the buying, not the urge.

wrong.The first trade at the opening bell: That's buying the urge at the bell. Our rule waits for the opening range to break.
wrong.The close of the first day: Some setups buy the close, but our Kicker entries are the prior day's high or the 30-minute range break.
wrong.Any dip below the open price: A dip under the open is not our trigger. The Kicker buys a break up through a level.

questions.q: The buy point was $40. You missed it, and it's trading at $43.60 now. How far past the buy point would you be paying?
questions.why: 9.0%. $43.60 minus $40 is $3.60. $3.60 over $40 is 9.0%. That's more than twice our 4% line, so I'm out on this one. The reason is the stop. It still lives under the $40 buy point, so the drop to it is long and your shares get small. And the further past the buy point you buy, the easier you get shaken out. Let it go, or wait for it to set up again.
questions.lesson_line: Measure how far past the buy point you are before you buy. Past 4%, let it go.
questions.simple: 9.0%. $43.60 is way past our 4% line over the $40 buy point, so it's a pass.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a 9% run proves the stock is strong, so buying it must be safe. It may be strong. But your stop still sits under the $40 buy point, so the drop to it is long. Past 4% above the buy point, we don't buy. Richard Rhodes' rule for a missed trade: wait for a correction before putting it on.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28 replaced IBD's 5% buy zone with 4%)
+1 fixed before (why reworded by the checker)

wrong.8.3%: Divided the gain by today's price. Measure from the buy point.
wrong.3.6%: That's the dollar gap, $3.60, read as a percent.

questions.story: You planned to buy the breakout over $40, stop $39. You got busy and missed it. Now it's $44, and you're kicking yourself.
questions.q: What's your move now?
choices: Wait for a pullback, higher low
Buy now, keep the old $39 stop
Wait for a new high, then buy
Buy double size to catch up
questions.answer: Wait for a pullback, higher low
questions.why: Wait for the pullback. At $44 you're way past 4% over the $40 buy point, so buying here is a chase. Do it off the old $39 stop and your risk per share is several times what you planned. Regret buys like this often land near a peak. So let it come back to you. If it pulls back and holds a higher low, that low is a fresh spot to risk against, with a tight stop.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the break: let it go, or wait for the pullback. Don't buy your regret.

wrong.Buy double size to catch up: Size can't fix a late entry. It just makes the chase bigger.
wrong.Wait for a new high, then buy: A new high is even further past the $40 buy point. That's more chase, not less.
wrong.Buy now, keep the old $39 stop: Old stop, much higher entry. Your risk per share is several times the plan.

questions.simple: Wait for a pullback that holds a higher low. A regret buy after a missed move often lands near a peak.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% line)
+1 a choice replaced in this batch (the stop-at-$43 choice and its overreaching note)

deeper.example: Richard Rhodes' trading rules on ChartSchool: be patient, and if a trade is missed, wait for a correction to occur before putting the trade on. Investopedia's trading psychology page notes that a regret entry after a missed move often loses as prices fall from their highs.

questions.q: Your journal shows your win rate drops on the days you trade the most. What does trading coach Brett Steenbarger find behind that?
choices: The extra trades are FOMO trades
Busy days are just harder markets
You need a faster trading platform
Your position size was too small
questions.answer: The extra trades are FOMO trades
questions.why: The extra trades are FOMO trades. Steenbarger calls it a common pattern. Win rate drops as the trade count climbs. Often it's because the added trades come from the fear of missing out. Those are the marginal ones, the so-so ideas you'd skip on a calm day. Check your own journal for it. Tag every trade that wasn't in your plan and compare its results with the rest.
questions.lesson_line: When your trade count jumps, check how many came from FOMO.

wrong.Busy days are just harder markets: Some may be, but the pattern he finds is in the trader. The added trades are the marginal ones.
wrong.You need a faster trading platform: Speed doesn't fix the choice to take a marginal trade.
wrong.Your position size was too small: Size doesn't change how often trades win. The extra trades were the weak ones.

questions.simple: The extra trades come from fear of missing out, and those added trades are the weak ones.

reasons: +1 fixed before (a fact replaced by the checker)

deeper.example: Investopedia's trading psychology page adds the other side: regret pulls traders into a move they missed, and that late entry often loses as prices fall from their highs.

questions.story: A stock you've watched gaps up 8% at the open on news. It's 9:32 and still running. You have no entry or stop planned.
questions.q: What's the disciplined move?
choices: Wait for the opening range to set
Buy at market before it runs away
Buy now, set a stop later
Short it, the gap is far too big
questions.answer: Wait for the opening range to set
questions.why: Wait for the opening range to form. With no entry or stop, you can't know your risk or size the trade. ChartSchool's gap rule allows one hour after the open for the price to set its range. Some traders watch only a few minutes. Then you have a level to buy over and a low for the stop. The SEC's line: never feel pressured to invest right away.
questions.lesson_line: No plan, no trade. Let the range form, then buy the break with a stop under it.

wrong.Buy at market before it runs away: The order type isn't the fault. Our entries are market orders too. Buying on urgency with no stop is the mistake.
wrong.Buy now, set a stop later: Without a stop you don't know your risk, so you can't size the trade.
wrong.Short it, the gap is far too big: A big gap is no reason to fight it. With no plan, the answer is to wait, not to flip sides.

questions.simple: Wait for the opening range to form, because with no plan you have no level to buy and no place for a stop.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a fast open as a reason to act now. A gap still running at 9:32 has set no range yet, so there is no level to buy over and no low for a stop. Without a stop you can't size the trade, and the loss has no floor. Waiting may cost some price. The range gives you both a trigger and a stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 in a wrong note; D39 and C30, see owner flag)
+1 fixed before (why changed by the checker)

questions.q: GameStop, early 2021. The hype topped it at $120.75. A few weeks later it traded at $10.97. How far down was a buyer at the top?
questions.why: About 91%. $120.75 minus $10.97 is $109.78. $109.78 over $120.75 is about 90.9%, call it 91%. That's what showing up last to a mania looks like. It ran from around $5 on social media hype. The people who bought the top because everyone was talking about it took the pain. Once a stock is all over your feeds, it's likely already run. You're not early.
questions.lesson_line: When the hype is everywhere, you're probably late.
questions.simple: About 91%. It fell from $120.75 to $10.97 within a few weeks of the top.

deeper.example: Investopedia's GameStop case: on social media hype in January 2021, the stock went from around $5 to about $120 in under three weeks. It topped at $120.75 and traded at $10.97 a few weeks later. Many who arrived late to the party endured significant pain.

reasons: +2 computed key from quoted history numbers
+1 fixed before (question reworded by the checker)

wrong.9%: That's what was left, not the fall.
wrong.1,001%: Divided the drop by the later price. Divide by the top.
wrong.110%: That's the $109.78 dollar drop read as a percent.

questions.story: A stock is all over your feeds. Up 40% in five days, friends posting their gains, and you don't own a share.
questions.q: How do you read this one?
choices: I'm late, wait for a real setup
The buzz says it goes higher
Buy now, add as it rises
Short it, it has to fall now
questions.answer: I'm late, wait for a real setup
questions.why: You're late. When everyone's talking about a stock, it has likely already run and gotten expensive. The early buyers are the ones posting gains, and they may be getting ready to sell to someone. Don't let that someone be you. If you're feeling the FOMO, so is everybody else, and the obvious trade is often not the good one. Put it on your list and wait for a real setup with a stop.
questions.lesson_line: If the whole internet knows about it, you're not early.

wrong.Short it, it has to fall now: A fast run can keep running. Shorting it with no setup is a guess.
wrong.Buy now, add as it rises: That's chasing twice. The full size goes on once, at one price, and adding as it runs is never the plan.
wrong.The buzz says it goes higher: Buzz is the crowd, not a signal. Following the crowd can lead to big losses.

questions.simple: You're late. Once everyone is talking about a stock it has likely already run, so wait for a real setup.

deeper.trap: The trap is that friends' gains feel like proof. They prove the stock already moved, not that it'll keep moving. Up 40% in five days, the honest read is that you're late. Brett Steenbarger's line: if you're feeling FOMO, others likely are too, and the obvious trade is often not the high-percentage one.

questions.q: Yesterday's low was $48.50. Today it gaps up 8% and you want in at $54, stop $48.45 under that low. How wide is that stop?
questions.why: 10.3%. $54 minus $48.45 is $5.55 a share. $5.55 over $54 is about 10.3%. Way too wide. We like a stop 1% to 3% away, and we'll take up to 5%. Past 5% we mostly wait for a tighter trigger. The size comes from the stop, so a 10.3% stop means a tiny position. That's FOMO's trap after a gap. Don't squeeze the stop to make it fit. Skip it, or wait for a tighter spot.
questions.lesson_line: After a gap, measure the stop before you buy. A wide stop means a small position, or no trade.
questions.simple: About 10.3%, way too wide. Don't squeeze the stop to fit, skip it or wait for a tighter spot.

deeper.trap: The trap is tightening the stop to make the gap trade fit. The stop goes a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, not where it feels small. If the honest stop doesn't fit your risk, you skip the trade. The gap was exciting. That's not a reason.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62: a few cents under the low)
+1 restated in this batch

wrong.11.5%: Divided by the stop price. Measure from your entry, $54.
wrong.89.7%: That's the stop as a share of the entry, not the distance to it.
wrong.18.3%: Added the 8% gap on top. The stop distance is just entry to stop.

questions.story: Your journal shows a pattern. You miss the planned entry, chase the move, and most of those end as small stop-outs.
questions.q: What fixes it at the root?
choices: Grade each day on your process
Trade more names so you miss less
Use wider stops on the chases
Buy before the signal to beat it
questions.answer: Grade each day on your process
questions.why: Grade each day on your process. You chase because a missed entry feels like a loss, so you go get it back. Score the day on whether you followed the plan, not on P&L. Now letting a missed trade go counts as a good day, and the chase counts as a bad one, even when it works. Change what counts as a win and the habit loses its fuel.
questions.lesson_line: Score your day on the process, not the P&L.

wrong.Trade more names so you miss less: More names means more moves to chase. You'll always miss some. The job is the best ones.
wrong.Use wider stops on the chases: The size comes from the stop, so a wider one just buys fewer shares. The chasing stays.
wrong.Buy before the signal to beat it: That's FOMO's other face, in before the signal on fear.

questions.simple: Grade each day on whether you followed your plan, not on the money you made.

deeper.counter: Wider stops and more names look like fixes but feed the same habit. The size comes from the stop, so a wider stop just buys fewer shares on a worse entry. More names means more moves to chase. Grading the process changes what counts as a win. A day you followed the plan is a good day, even with no trade.
deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger coached a portfolio manager who watched the market move away from his ideal entry and chased it. All too often that led to paper-cut losses. The fix: he graded himself at the end of each day purely on process.

reasons: +1 key text shortened in this batch to remove a longest-choice tell

questions.q: You missed a breakout and watched it run without you. That miss cost your account nothing.
questions.why: True. Your account's right where it was. You gave up a gain you might've had, that's all. The real damage from a miss happens in your head. Count it as a loss and you'll chase the next one to win it back. That's how a miss turns into a real loss. Not having a position is a position. No setup, no trade. Another one will come along.
questions.lesson_line: A missed trade leaves your account whole. A chased one can cost plenty.
questions.simple: True. A miss takes nothing from your account, you just give up a gain you might have had.

deeper.trap: The trap is counting a missed gain as a loss. Do that and every move you missed feels like money owed, and the urge to chase grows. Your account is whole, and other trades keep showing up later in the day or the next day.
deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger: the danger in missing trades isn't financial risk, it's the self-criticism after. Richard Rhodes: not having a position is a position.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D44, cash is a position)
+1 statement flipped to True in this batch for the unit's True/False balance

questions.story: You missed the breakout over $40. It ran to $45, then pulled back to $41, held above its last low, and turned up.
questions.q: You buy the turn near $41, stop just under the pullback low. Is that a chase?
choices: No, it's a pullback near support
Yes, it already broke out at $40
Yes, only new highs are safe
No, any dip after a breakout is a buy
questions.answer: No, it's a pullback near support
questions.why: Not a chase. That's your second chance. It broke out over $40, ran to $45, and came back without breaking its last low. A higher low, sitting right on top of the old breakout level. The old ceiling around $40 is acting as support now. Your stop goes just under that pullback low, so the risk is small. And $41 is still inside 4% of the $40 buy point.
questions.lesson_line: Miss the break, wait for the pullback that holds. That's your second chance.

wrong.Yes, it already broke out at $40: A missed breakout isn't gone. Waiting for the pullback and buying it is exactly the fix.
wrong.Yes, only new highs are safe: Buying near support with a close stop is the better spot. A new high far from support means a wider stop.
wrong.No, any dip after a breakout is a buy: Not any dip. This one counts because it held above its last low. An uptrend needs higher lows.

questions.simple: Not a chase. You bought a pullback that held above its last low, right near the old breakout.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a missed breakout is gone for good. Here it broke out over $40, ran to $45 and came back to $41, above its last low. That's a second chance near support, with a stop close by. It stops being this setup if the dip breaks its last low, because an uptrend needs higher lows.
deeper.example: John Murphy's laws on ChartSchool: the best place to buy is near support, and a broken resistance peak will often act as support on later pullbacks. Richard Rhodes: if a trade is missed, wait for a correction before putting it on.

reasons: +1 fixed before (question wording changed by the checker)

questions.story: You've chased three moves this week and been stopped out of all three. You're angry. Another stock is ripping and you feel the pull.
questions.q: What's our call for the rest of today?
choices: Done for today, no new trades
Buy it, this one makes it back
Take a short break, then trade it
Enter, but with a very tight stop
questions.answer: Done for today, no new trades
questions.why: Done for today. Angry means no new trades, and we hold tired, sick and distracted to the same line. After three stop-outs that pull isn't a setup. It's the urge to win the money back. That urge is how a bad week turns into a bad month. Shut the screen, journal the three trades, and come back tomorrow with a written plan. The setups will still be there.
questions.lesson_line: Angry after a run of losses means you're done for the day. Step away from the screen.

wrong.Enter, but with a very tight stop: Angry means no new trades, stop or no stop. And chasers get whipsawed and stopped out a lot.
wrong.Take a short break, then trade it: A breather isn't enough. Angry means no new trades for the rest of the day.
wrong.Buy it, this one makes it back: That's trading to win money back, not trading a setup.

questions.simple: No new trades today. You're angry after three chased losses, and the pull is emotion, not a setup.

deeper.trap: The trap is the tight stop. It feels like it caps the damage, so the chase seems safe. But traders who chase out of FOMO get whipsawed and stopped out a lot. One more stop-out feeds the urge to win it back. The fix isn't a better order. It's no new trades today.
deeper.example: Bob Farrell's rules on ChartSchool: when emotions run high, take a breather and step back. Richard Rhodes: the urge to get the money back is extreme and should not be given in to. Our line goes further than a breather.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (F67, no new trades that day)
+1 fixed before (openers varied by the checker)
+1 key and story changed in this batch

questions.q: Your job as a trader is to be in as many of the big moves as you can.
questions.why: False. You'll miss big moves all the time. I do too. Chase every one and you end up buying late, far from your stop, over and over. The job is to limit your risk and take the best setups, then trade those as well as you can. A few clean trades beat a pile of late ones. Steady profits matter more than being in every mover. No setup, no trade. Cash is a position too.
questions.lesson_line: You'll miss plenty of moves. Your job is the best few, done well.
questions.simple: False. Nobody catches every move, so your job is to limit risk and trade the best few well.

deeper.trap: The trap is grading yourself on the moves you missed. That turns every big move into a target, and chasing movers costs you consistency. Pick the best few, limit the risk on each, and let the rest go.
deeper.example: Brett Steenbarger: the goal isn't to trade every possible opportunity, but to find the best ones and trade those as well as possible. ChartSchool's gap-trading page: it's more important to be consistently profitable than to chase movers.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D44, no setup, no trade)
+1 fixed before (statement reworded by the checker)

questions.q: You're late to a breakout. How far over the buy point will we still pay up for it?
choices: Up to 4% over the buy point
Up to 5% over the buy point
Up to 10% over the buy point
Any price, if I cut my shares
questions.answer: Up to 4% over the buy point
questions.simple: Up to 4%. Past that we don't buy, because the stop is too far below and the shares get too small.
questions.why: 4%, and not a penny more. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Inside that, you can still buy, but the stop stays under the buy point. So the higher you pay, the wider your risk per share and the fewer shares you get. Past 4%, the trade's gotten too expensive for what it gives you. Let it go or wait for the next setup.
questions.lesson_line: Our chase line is 4% above the buy point. Past it, we don't buy.

wrong.Up to 5% over the buy point: That's IBD's buy zone. Ours is tighter, 4%.
wrong.Up to 10% over the buy point: That's a different check, how stretched it is over the 9 EMA. The buy-point line is 4%.
wrong.Any price, if I cut my shares: Fewer shares is the cost of paying up inside 4%. Past 4%, we don't buy at all.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, C29)
+1 new in this batch

deeper.example: IBD talks about a 5% buy zone after a breakout, and says the further past the buy point you get in, the greater the risk of getting shaken out. Our line is tighter, at 4%.

questions.story: Last night you wrote the plan: buy over $50, stop $49.20, size set. This morning it clears $50 and trades at $50.60. You worry it's already a chase.
questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Yes, buy now at market
No, wait for a pullback
Half now, half on a dip
Limit order back at $50
questions.simple: Yes, buy it. The trigger hit, the price is still inside our 4% line, and the plan was set last night.
questions.why: Yes, buy it now at market. This isn't a chase. It's your plan triggering. You wrote it last night, it cleared $50, and $50.60 is well inside our 4% line. We use market orders for entries. One thing changes: the stop's still $49.20, so your risk per share is bigger than planned. Rework the size off your real fill. Fewer shares, same dollar risk.
questions.lesson_line: Your written trigger hits inside 4%: buy it. That's the plan, not a chase.

wrong.No, wait for a pullback: Nothing was missed. $50.60 is right at your trigger, well inside 4%. Buying strength here is the plan.
wrong.Half now, half on a dip: No starter piece. The full size goes on at one price with one stop. Buying more on a dip under your fill is adding to a loser.
wrong.Limit order back at $50: We use market orders for entries. A limit at $50 can leave you out of the trade you planned.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D39, C28, E57, A5)
+1 new in this batch

deeper.trap: The trap is treating every fast move as a chase. A chase is buying far past the buy point. Here the price sits just over the trigger you wrote last night, well inside our 4% line. Buy it, and size from the stop at the real price. Risk per share is bigger than planned, so you buy fewer shares. You don't skip the trade.

questions.story: A stock you've watched gaps up 8% at the open on news. It's 9:32 and still running. You have no entry or stop planned.
questions.q: What's the play?
choices: Skip today and plan it tonight
Buy at market before it runs
Buy now, set a stop later
Short it, the gap is too big
questions.answer: Skip today and plan it tonight
questions.simple: Skip it today. With no entry, stop or size written before the open, you can't know your risk.
questions.why: Skip it today. Write the plan tonight. Every buy we make has its entry, stop and size on paper before the open, and this one has none. With no stop you don't know your risk, so you can't size it. You'd be buying on adrenaline. The fear says it's now or never. It isn't. If it still looks good tonight, plan it for tomorrow. New setups keep coming.
questions.lesson_line: No written plan before the open, no buy. Plan it tonight if it still looks good.

wrong.Buy at market before it runs: Market orders are fine, we use them. Buying on urgency with no plan is the mistake.
wrong.Buy now, set a stop later: The size comes from the stop. With no stop you can't know your risk or size it.
wrong.Short it, the gap is too big: A big gap is no reason to fight it. No setup, no trade, either side.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D39; see the owner flag on D39 and the day-one opening-range entry)
+2 replaces q17, whose key taught the web view D39 replaced

deeper.trap: The trap is reading a fast open as a reason to act now. We write every buy's entry, stop and size before the open. A stock you never planned has none of those, so you can't size it. Let it go today. If it still looks good tonight, write the plan for tomorrow.

conflicts: Opening range length: Investopedia defines the opening range as the first 15 minutes (and says some traders watch an hour or more), ChartSchool's gap rule waits one hour, and our Kicker rule uses the 30-minute range. The file keys no universal length: q17's key is 'wait for the opening range to form', and only q13 named a length, as our Kicker rule (q13 is now cut, so no live question names one).

Buying strength: Rhodes (ChartSchool) says buy what shows strength; Investopedia's 'Chasing the Market' says momentum strategies can succeed chasing trends; Steenbarger's 'Why FOMO Fails' says chasing strength in a trend without momentum gets whipsawed. The file never keys 'buying strength is bad'; q06 keys only that buying strength at a planned trigger is not the same as chasing late.

The SEC's hot-stock alert and its Behavioral Patterns bulletin list 'momentum investing' and 'noise trading' (which 'follow trends') among behaviours that can undermine results. UCT trades momentum swing setups, so the file uses those SEC pages only for crowd-following, FOMO, pressure and manias, and never keys momentum or trend-following as a mistake.
The two Director's Take pages (s1, s4) are archived ('no longer being updated'); they are used only for timeless points (FOMO, others buying, pressure tactics).

IBD's 5% buy zone (q06, q14): the article is paywalled after its first paragraph; only the headline and first paragraph are quoted. 'Ends 5% past the buy point' is read from the headline plus the first paragraph and is asked as IBD's convention, not a law.

Unit row: the plan says the cure is 'the firm's "want to see a higher low"'. That phrase is not in an allowed house source (sizing_rule.md owner lines, TRADE_PLANS.md, OWNER_PRINCIPLES.md quotes); VOICE.md has owner-register lines ('Buying the flagpole instead of waiting for the flag') but is not a house source under the contract.
